Severe Floods Sweep Argentina, Disrupting Key Economic Sectors

Widespread flooding across central and northern Argentina is causing significant disruption to transport, agriculture, and retail as heavy rains continue for a fifth consecutive day. Rivers in the provinces of Santa Fe, Córdoba, and Entre Ríos burst their banks following torrential downpours, inundating homes, farmland, and industrial zones in one of the country’s most economically vital regions.

Local authorities estimate that over 25,000 people have been displaced, with emergency shelters filling rapidly. The National Meteorological Service (SMN) reported that some areas have received more than 250 millimeters of rain since Monday, overwhelming drainage systems and complicating rescue efforts. Several highways and rural roads, crucial for the movement of goods, remain underwater or blocked by debris.

Governor Lucía Navarro of Santa Fe spoke from a relief center in Rafaela: “This is the worst flooding our province has seen in over two decades. We are prioritizing the safety of residents, but we are acutely aware of the impact this will have on harvests and local businesses.”

The timing of the floods has raised particular concern within Argentina’s massive agricultural sector. The Chamber of Grain Producers warned that the situation could jeopardize the ongoing soybean and corn harvests, with waterlogged fields rendering machinery inoperable and risking crop loss. “Early estimates suggest that up to 15% of this season’s soybeans in affected areas could be lost if the water does not recede soon,” said spokesperson Martín Aguirre.

Urban centers are also feeling the effects. In Rosario and Córdoba, local supermarkets have reported shortages of fresh produce and dairy products as deliveries are delayed or canceled. The Union of Road Transport Workers stated that at least 350 truck routes have been suspended across the three provinces. “Our drivers are stranded, and supply chains are under severe stress,” said union leader Carla Ocampo.

Industrial parks in the outskirts of Santa Fe city and Córdoba have been forced to halt production, as employees struggle to reach work and warehouses face flooding. Fernando Paz, an economic analyst at the Regional Institute for Economic Studies, commented: “It’s too early to calculate the full cost, but the disruption to logistics and manufacturing will ripple through the national economy for weeks.”

With weather forecasts predicting continued rain through the weekend, emergency services are bracing for further challenges. National authorities have pledged additional resources, but officials warn that recovery will depend on conditions improving. As the waters rise, Argentina faces mounting economic and humanitarian pressures.
